questions.question: You need to distribute TCP 1433 traffic from application servers to three database VMs. The database endpoint must not be reachable from the internet. What should you deploy?

options.text: A Standard internal load balancer
options.why: Correct. An internal load balancer uses a private frontend IP in the virtual network.

options.text: A Standard public load balancer
options.why: A public frontend is reachable from the internet.

options.text: An Azure Application Gateway
options.why: Application Gateway is a layer 7 HTTP load balancer and does not suit TCP 1433.

options.text: Azure Front Door
options.why: Front Door is a global HTTP service with a public endpoint.

questions.explanation: An internal load balancer frontend has a private IP address that is reachable only from the virtual network, peered networks and connected on-premises networks.

questions.question: A Standard load balancer marks VM2 in the backend pool as unhealthy. The web application on VM2 works when tested locally. An NSG on the NIC of VM2 contains a deny rule. Which traffic is the deny rule most likely blocking?

options.text: Traffic from the AzureLoadBalancer service tag (168.63.129.16)
options.why: Correct. Health probes originate from 168.63.129.16, and blocking them marks the backend as unhealthy.

options.text: Traffic from the VirtualNetwork service tag
options.why: Health probes do not originate from the virtual network address space.

options.text: Outbound traffic to the Internet service tag
options.why: Probe responses are return traffic and are allowed automatically by the stateful NSG.

options.text: Traffic from the GatewayManager service tag
options.why: GatewayManager is used for gateway and Bastion management.

questions.explanation: Allow inbound traffic from the AzureLoadBalancer service tag. The default rule AllowAzureLoadBalancerInBound does this unless a lower-numbered rule denies it.

questions.question: A Standard public load balancer has a load-balancing rule for TCP 80, a healthy HTTP probe and two backend VMs. Neither the VM network interfaces nor their subnet has an NSG. Clients cannot connect. What should you do?

options.text: Associate an NSG that allows inbound TCP 80 with the subnet or the network interfaces
options.why: Correct. A Standard load balancer is secure by default, so an NSG must allow the traffic.

options.text: Change the load balancer to the Basic SKU
options.why: The Basic SKU is retired.

options.text: Add an inbound NAT rule for TCP 80
options.why: Inbound NAT rules forward to one VM and are also subject to the same requirement.

options.text: Enable floating IP on the rule
options.why: Floating IP changes the destination address seen by the VM and does not allow traffic.

questions.explanation: Standard load balancers and Standard public IP addresses are closed to inbound flows unless an NSG explicitly allows them.

questions.question: Users of a web application must be sent to the same backend VM for every request from the same client IP address. Which load-balancing rule setting should you configure?

options.text: Session persistence set to Client IP
options.why: Correct. This uses a 2-tuple hash of the source and destination IP addresses.

options.text: Session persistence set to None
options.why: None uses a 5-tuple hash, so a new source port can reach a different VM.

options.text: Floating IP enabled
options.why: Floating IP does not affect which VM receives the traffic.

options.text: A TCP health probe
options.why: Probes check health and do not control distribution.

questions.explanation: Session persistence Client IP (2-tuple) or Client IP and protocol (3-tuple) keeps a client on the same backend.

questions.question: An HTTP health probe is configured for port 80 and the path /status. Every backend VM is marked unhealthy. The web server on each VM listens on port 80 and returns HTTP 404 for /status. Which two actions would resolve the issue? Each correct answer presents a complete solution.

options.text: Change the probe path to a page that returns HTTP 200
options.why: Correct. An HTTP probe treats only a 200 response as healthy.

options.text: Change the probe protocol to TCP on port 80
options.why: Correct. A TCP probe succeeds when the port accepts connections.

options.text: Increase the probe interval
options.why: The interval changes how often the probe runs, not the result.

options.text: Add the VMs to a second backend pool
options.why: The same probe would still fail.

questions.explanation: HTTP and HTTPS probes require a 200 response. A TCP probe checks only that the port accepts a connection.
